lesson.title: Pulling Constants Out: The Constant Multiple Rule for Integrals
lesson.summary: A constant factor can always be pulled outside an integral sign, a shortcut that turns messy looking integrals into simple ones you already know how to solve.
lesson.body:
The constant multiple rule for integrals says that for any constant k, the integral of k times f(x) equals k times the integral of f(x): integral of k*f(x) dx = k * integral of f(x) dx. In words, a number multiplying the whole function can be moved outside the integral sign and dealt with separately.

This rule is not a new fact you have to memorize from scratch. It falls straight out of the constant multiple rule for derivatives, run backward. You already know that if F(x) is a function and k is a constant, then the derivative of k*F(x) is k*F'(x), because differentiation distributes over a constant factor. Now suppose F is an antiderivative of f, meaning F'(x) = f(x). Then the derivative of k*F(x) is k*f(x), which means k*F(x) is an antiderivative of k*f(x). That is exactly the constant multiple rule for integrals, discovered by reading a derivative fact from right to left instead of left to right.

Recall that an indefinite integral, integral of f(x) dx, stands for the entire family of antiderivatives of f, written as F(x) + C. When you pull a constant out, that constant multiplies the whole family, but the arbitrary constant C absorbs the scaling, so you can still just write a single +C at the end rather than k*C. This is why the rule is usually written as k * integral of f(x) dx, with the understanding that the +C gets added once, at the very end.

Here is a worked example. Consider integral of 7*x^2 dx. Using the constant multiple rule, pull the 7 outside: 7 * integral of x^2 dx. The integral of x^2 dx is x^3/3 + C by the power rule for integration. Multiplying through gives 7*(x^3/3) + C, which simplifies to (7/3)*x^3 + C. To check this answer, differentiate it: the derivative of (7/3)*x^3 is (7/3)*3*x^2 = 7*x^2, which matches the original integrand exactly, confirming the antiderivative is correct.

One important caution: this rule only works for constant factors, numbers that do not depend on x. You cannot pull a variable factor like x itself outside an integral sign, since integral of x*f(x) dx is generally not equal to x * integral of f(x) dx. Keeping that distinction clear now will save confusion later, once integration techniques for products of functions are introduced.
